SECTION: Women and Men in STEM Often at Odds Over Workplace Equity (Pages 6-24)

TOPICS: gender discrimination, sexual harassment, workplace equity, racial/ethnic disparities, gender representation, job preferences, public perception, educational attainment, demographic composition

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- Women in STEM jobs are more likely to experience gender discrimination (50%) compared to men (19%), with higher rates among those in majority-male workplaces (78%), computer jobs (74%), or with postgraduate degrees (62%) (Page 6)
- 36% of women in STEM report sexual harassment as a problem in their workplace, compared to 28% of men (Page 6)
- Women in STEM are more likely to experience discrimination (50%) than women in non-STEM jobs (41%), but face similar levels of sexual harassment (Page 7)
- The share of women in STEM jobs has remained at about half since 1990, with an average of 14% across occupations (Page 7)
- Women's representation in computer occupations decreased from 32% in 1990 to 25% today (Page 8)
- Black STEM workers report experiencing racial/ethnic discrimination at work at a rate of 62%, significantly higher than other groups (Page 8)
- 50% of women in STEM jobs have experienced some form of gender discrimination, compared to 41% of women in non-STEM jobs and 19% of men in STEM (Page 9)
- Women in STEM working in majority-male workplaces are more likely to experience gender discrimination (78%) and feel their gender has made it harder to succeed (48%) (Page 10)
- Women with postgraduate degrees in STEM are more likely to experience gender discrimination (62%) and believe their gender has hindered their success (35%) compared to those with less education (Page 11)
- 74% of women in computer jobs report experiencing gender-related discrimination, compared to 16% of men (Page 12)
- 22% of working women in the U.S. say they have experienced sexual harassment at work, compared to 7% of men (Page 13)
- Women in STEM are more likely than men to regard sexual harassment as a problem in their workplace (36% vs. 28%), especially in majority-male settings (48%) and computer jobs (42%) (Page 13)
- 62% of black STEM workers report experiencing discrimination due to their race or ethnicity, compared to 42% of Hispanics and 13% of whites (Page 14)
- Black STEM workers are less likely than white workers to perceive fair treatment in hiring (43% vs. 78%) and promotions (37% vs. 75%) (Page 15)
- Employment in STEM occupations grew 79% since 1990, from 9.7 million to 17.3 million, with computer occupations seeing the largest growth at 338% (Page 16)
- Women account for a majority of healthcare practitioners and technicians (75%) but are underrepresented in computer (25%) and engineering (14%) positions (Page 16)
- Women make up 41% of STEM workers with professional or doctoral degrees (Page 17)
- Blacks make up 9% of STEM workers (vs. 11% of the U.S. workforce), Hispanics 7% (vs. 16%), while Asians are overrepresented at 17% of college-educated STEM workers (vs. 10% of all college-educated workers) (Page 17)
- About 69% of women who majored in health professions work in health-related occupations, compared to 61% of men; women are less likely than men to work in computer (38% vs. 53%) or engineering (24% vs. 30%) jobs (Page 18)
- 71% of U.S. adults see STEM jobs as offering better compensation, and 58% consider them to attract more qualified young people (Page 19)
- Women in STEM are more likely than men to prioritize jobs focused on helping others (59% vs. 31%), while men value higher pay and promotion opportunities more (Page 20)
- 39% of Americans consider lack of encouragement a major reason for fewer women in STEM, while 41% cite this for blacks and Hispanics; 42% believe limited access to quality education is a major factor for underrepresentation of blacks and Hispanics (Page 21)
- 72% of Black STEM workers believe racial/ethnic discrimination is a major reason for underrepresentation, compared to 27% of whites and 28% of Asians; 48% of women in STEM cite gender discrimination as a major factor (Page 22)
- 25% of Americans rate K-12 STEM education as above average, while 43% rate it as average and 30% as below average (Page 23)
- STEM employment grew 79% since 1990, with computer jobs increasing by 338%; women make up 50% of all STEM workers overall, but are underrepresented in computer (25%) and engineering (14%) jobs (Page 24)
- The gender wage gap is wider in STEM occupations than in non-STEM jobs (Page 24)

SECTION: 1. Diversity in the STEM workforce varies widely across jobs (Pages 24-46)

TOPICS: diversity in STEM workforce, gender representation, racial/ethnic representation, educational attainment, earnings disparities, employment outcomes, public perceptions

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- Women make up 50% of all U.S. workers in STEM occupations, but are underrepresented in computer and engineering jobs despite gains in life and physical sciences (Page 24)
- Black and Hispanic workers are underrepresented in STEM, making up 9% and 7% of STEM workers respectively, compared to their 11% and 16% share of the overall workforce (Page 24)
- Asians are overrepresented in STEM, particularly among college-educated workers at 17% (Page 24)
- STEM employment grew 79% (9.7 million to 17.3 million) since 1990, with computer jobs seeing a 338% increase (Page 24)
- Women's share in computer occupations has decreased by 7 percentage points since 1990 (Page 24)
- Among college-educated workers, 33% majored in STEM, but only 52% of those with STEM training are employed in STEM jobs (Page 25)
- Women who majored in computer science or engineering are less likely than men trained in those fields to be working in related jobs (Page 25)
- The analysis uses a broad definition of the STEM workforce based on occupation from the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey, including 74 occupations such as computer and mathematical roles, engineers, scientists, and health-related jobs (Page 26)
- Health-related jobs comprise 52% of the STEM workforce, totaling 9.0 million workers (Page 26)
- As of 2016, 17.3 million workers were employed in STEM occupations, making up 13% of the total workforce (Page 27)
- About half of STEM workers (52%, 9.0 million) are employed as health care practitioners and technicians (Page 27)
- Computer workers account for 25% (4.4 million) of STEM employment (Page 27)
- Employment of physical scientists has fallen by 46% from the 1990 level (Page 27)
- STEM workers are about twice as likely as non-STEM workers to have earned at least a bachelor's degree (65% vs. 32%) (Page 28)
- Roughly three-in-ten STEM workers (29%) have earned a master's, doctorate, or professional degree (Page 28)
- 54% of life scientists have an advanced degree (Page 28)
- 66% of STEM workers work for a private, for-profit employer (Page 29)
- Engineers and architects (82%) and computer workers (77%) are most likely to work for a private employer (Page 29)
- Only 6% of STEM workers are self-employed, compared to 11% of non-STEM workers (Page 29)
- Women comprise 47% of all employed adults today, up from 45% in 1990 (Page 30)
- Three-quarters (75%) of healthcare practitioners and technicians are women (Page 30)
- Women's representation in computer jobs has declined since 1990 (Page 30)
- Black and Hispanic workers are underrepresented in STEM overall and among those with professional or doctoral degrees (Page 30)
- Asians are overrepresented across all STEM occupational clusters, especially in computer occupations relative to their share among employed college graduates (Page 30)
- Women comprise 14% of workers in engineering occupations (Page 31)
- Women make up 25% of workers in computer occupations, down from 32% in 1990 (Page 31)
- Women represent 39% of physical scientists, 47% of life scientists, and 46% of math workers (Page 31)
- Among college-educated workers, 81% of those who majored in health professions are women, while only 16% of engineering majors are women (Page 31)
- Mechanical engineering and electrical engineering have the lowest shares of women at 8% and 9%, respectively (Page 31)
- Women make up 29% of environmental engineers, 26% of architects, and 21% of industrial engineers (Page 32)
- 89% of nurses and 95% of dental hygienists are women (Page 32)

- Three-quarters of Americans say they liked science classes in grades K-12, while only one-quarter say they disliked them (Page 91)

- Among those who disliked science classes, 61% cite the subject matter as the main reason, versus 36% who cite teaching (Page 91)
- 41% of STEM workers have an older family member in STEM, compared to 26% of non-STEM workers (Page 91)
- 44% of women in STEM jobs and 37% of men say they have or had a close older family member working in STEM (Page 91)

- 61% of those who liked math classes cited the subject matter as the main reason (Page 93)
- 59% of those who disliked math classes cited the subject matter as the main reason (Page 93)

- 11% say they liked math but not science; 29% disliked math but liked science; 14% disliked both (Page 94)
- Men are more likely than women to say they liked both math and science (54% vs. 39%) (Page 94)

- Whites, blacks, and Hispanics are about equally likely to say they liked both math and science classes (Page 94)
- There are no significant differences by age (Page 94)

- Among those holding a postgraduate degree in other fields, half (50%) say they liked both science and math classes (Page 95)
- Four-in-ten Americans in non-STEM jobs (40%) were "very" (16%) or "somewhat" (24%) interested in a STEM career (Page 96)
- About half (48%) were not too (21%) or not at all (27%) interested (Page 96)

- 28% were interested during high school or their teenage years (Page 97)
- 10% were interested in childhood/elementary school (Page 97)

SECTION: Methodology (Pages 102-105)

TOPICS: survey design, data sources, sampling strategy, weighting methodology, margin of error, response rates, classification, error sources, organizational information

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The analysis uses two sources: Pew Research Center analysis of IPUMS and decennial censuses, and a 2017 survey (Page 102)
- The survey was conducted from July 11 to Aug. 10, 2017, among 4,914 adults 18 years or older (Page 102)
- The margin of error for the full sample is +/- 2.7 percentage points (Page 102)
- The survey was conducted by the GfK Group using KnowledgePanel, which recruits members via probability sampling, including those without internet access (Page 102)
- KnowledgePanel uses a combination of RDD and ABS methodologies for recruitment (Page 102)
- The survey sampled about 2,500 STEM-employed panelists, 1,900 non-STEM-employed panelists, and 500 general public panelists (Page 103)
- 8,995 panelists were invited to participate, with a completion rate of 62.9% and a cumulative response rate of 5% (Page 103)
- All respondents verified their current employment status, and updated occupation data was collected for those whose job had changed (Page 103)
- Most STEM workers were asked to describe their job in detail for final classification (Page 103)
- STEM occupations included computer and mathematical, architecture and engineering, life and physical sciences, medical doctors, other health care practitioners, health care technologists and technicians, and teachers (Page 103)
- The survey classified healthcare support occupations and all other categories as non-STEM jobs (Page 104)
- The sample of Asians in STEM jobs includes only those proficient in English due to the survey being conducted in English and Spanish (Page 104)
- Data were weighted in a multistep process starting with a base weight for selection probability (Page 104)
- Respondents were divided into four mutually exclusive subgroups: 1) STEM workers (excluding STEM teachers), 2) non-STEM workers (excluding non-STEM teachers), 3) Teachers (both STEM and non-STEM), 4) Non-workers (Page 104)
- Each subgroup was separately weighted using an iterative technique to match population benchmarks (Page 104)
- The final step combined workers and non-workers, adjusting weights so their relative proportions and demographic profiles matched estimates for all U.S. adults (Page 104)
- Population benchmarks included gender by age, race/ethnicity, education, household income, region by metropolitan status, and primary language (Page 104)
- Primary language parameters come from the Census Bureau's 2015 American Community Survey; all other parameters come from the March 2016 Current Population Survey (CPS) (Page 104)
- Sampling errors and tests of statistical significance account for the effect of weighting at each stage (Page 104)
- Tables show unweighted sample sizes and error attributable to sampling at the 95% confidence level (Page 104)
- Sample sizes and sampling errors for other subgroups are available upon request (Page 104)
- Question wording and practical difficulties in conducting surveys can introduce error or bias into the findings of opinion polls (Page 105)

pages.ocr_text: Terminology The data in this report come from two sources: 1) a Pew Research Center analysis of the U.S. Census Bureau's 1990 and 2000 decennial censuses as well as aggregated 2014-2016 American Community Survey data and 2) a nationally representative survey of 4,914 U.S. adults, ages 18 and older, conducted July 11-Aug. 10, 2017. The survey, which was conducted online in English and Spanish through GfK's Knowledge Panel, included an oversample of employed adults working in science, technology, engineering and math (STEM) jobs. Analysis of the survey data compares those working in STEM jobs with those in non-STEM jobs based on self-identified occupation. STEM jobs include: computer and mathematical jobs, architecture and engineering, life sciences, physical sciences, healthcare practitioners and technicians, and teachers at the K-12 or postsecondary level with a specialty in teaching science, technology, engineering or math subjects. A similar definition is used to identify the STEM workforce in the U.S. Census Bureau data based on the 2010 Standard Occupational Classification. However, no educators are included as having STEM jobs in that data because the dataset does not allow identification of educators with a subject matter expertise in STEM subjects. References to the STEM workforce are based on those employed in a job classified as being in science, technology, engineering or math. Some analysis of the U.S. Census Bureau data compares those with a college degree who majored in STEM and those who majored in other fields. A STEM major includes the following areas: computers, mathematics and statistics, biological, agricultural and environmental sciences, physical and earth sciences, engineering, architecture, health-related fields, such as nursing, and STEM education, like science or math teacher education. Some analysis of the survey data is based on those with a postgraduate degree in a STEM field, using the same definition as above. References to whites, blacks and Asians include only those who are non-Hispanic and identify themselves as only one race. Hispanics are of any race. Asians working in STEM jobs are based on those who self-identify as Asian or Asian American and work in occupations classified as STEM. There are too few Asians working in non-STEM jobs in the survey for separate analysis. Note that the survey was conducted in English and Spanish only; thus only Asians proficient in English/Spanish are likely to have completed the survey. For more

STEM jobs include: computer and mathematical jobs, architecture and engineering, life sciences, physical sciences, healthcare practitioners and technicians, and teachers at the K-12 or postsecondary level with a specialty in teaching science, technology, engineering or math subjects.

A similar definition is used to identify the STEM workforce in the U.S. Census Bureau data based on the 2010 Standard Occupational Classification. However, no educators are included as having STEM jobs in that data because the dataset does not allow identification of educators with a subject matter expertise in STEM subjects.
References to the STEM workforce are based on those employed in a job classified as being in science, technology, engineering or math.

Some analysis of the U.S. Census Bureau data compares those with a college degree who majored in STEM and those who majored in other fields. A STEM major includes the following areas: computers, mathematics and statistics, biological, agricultural and environmental sciences, physical and earth sciences, engineering, architecture, health-related fields, such as nursing, and STEM education, like science or math teacher education. Some analysis of the survey data is based on those with a postgraduate degree in a STEM field, using the same definition as above.
References to whites, blacks and Asians include only those who are non-Hispanic and identify themselves as only one race. Hispanics are of any race.

Asians working in STEM jobs are based on those who self-identify as Asian or Asian American and work in occupations classified as STEM. There are too few Asians working in non-STEM jobs in the survey for separate analysis. Note that the survey was conducted in English and Spanish only; thus only Asians proficient in English/Spanish are likely to have completed the survey. For more

This page from a Pew Research Center report examines workplace equity in STEM fields, highlighting that women in these roles—particularly those in majority-male workplaces, computer jobs, or with postgraduate degrees—perceive higher levels of gender discrimination and sexual harassment compared to their male counterparts. The main content includes a detailed bar chart showing the percentage of STEM workers who have experienced gender discrimination, felt their gender hindered career success, or reported sexual harassment as a problem. The data is based on a nationally representative survey conducted from July 11 to August 10, 2017, and reveals significant disparities between men and women in STEM.

**Text Evidence:**
- Women in STEM jobs are more likely to experience gender discrimination, with 50% reporting it compared to 19% of men.
- A majority of women in STEM with postgraduate degrees (62%), in computer jobs (74%), and in mostly male workplaces (78%) have experienced gender discrimination.
- 36% of women in STEM report that sexual harassment is a problem in their workplace, compared to 28% of men.
- The survey was conducted in the summer of 2017, prior to recent public outcry about sexual harassment.

elements.text: Women and Men in STEM Often at Odds Over Workplace Equity
Perceived inequities are especially common among women in science, technology, engineering and math jobs who work mostly with men

For women working in science, technology, engineering or math (STEM) jobs, the workplace is a different, sometimes more hostile environment than the one their male coworkers experience. Discrimination and sexual harassment are seen as more frequent, and gender is perceived as more of an impediment than an advantage to career success. Three groups of women in STEM jobs stand out as more likely to see workplace inequities: women employed in STEM settings where men outnumber women, women working in computer jobs (only some of whom work in the technology industry), and women in STEM who hold postgraduate degrees. Indeed, a majority of each of these groups of STEM women have experienced gender discrimination at work, according to a nationally representative Pew Research Center survey with an oversample of people working in STEM jobs.

These findings come amid heightened public debate about underrepresentation and treatment of women – as well as racial and ethnic minorities – in the fast-growing technology industry and decades of concern about how best to promote diversity and inclusion in the STEM workforce. SECTION: Women and Men in STEM Often at Odds Over Workplace Equity (Pages 6-24)

TOPICS: gender discrimination, sexual harassment, workplace equity, racial/ethnic disparities, gender representation, job preferences, public perception, educational attainment, demographic composition

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- Women in STEM jobs are more likely to experience gender discrimination (50%) compared to men (19%), with higher rates among those in majority-male workplaces (78%), computer jobs (74%), or with postgraduate degrees (62%) (Page 6)
- 36% of women in STEM report sexual harassment as a problem in their workplace, compared to 28% of men (Page 6)
- Women in STEM are more likely to experience discrimination (50%) than women in non-STEM jobs (41%), but face similar levels of sexual harassment (Page 7)
- The share of women in STEM jobs has remained at about half since 1990, with an average of 14% across occupations (Page 7)
- Women's representation in computer occupations decreased from 32% in 1990 to 25% today (Page 8)
- Black STEM workers report experiencing racial/ethnic discrimination at work at a rate of 62%, significantly higher than other groups (Page 8)
- 50% of women in STEM jobs have experienced some form of gender discrimination, compared to 41% of women in non-STEM jobs and 19% of men in STEM (Page 9)
- Women in STEM working in majority-male workplaces are more likely to experience gender discrimination (78%) and feel their gender has made it harder to succeed (48%) (Page 10)
- Women with postgraduate degrees in STEM are more likely to experience gender discrimination (62%) and believe their gender has hindered their success (35%) compared to those with less education (Page 11)
- 74% of women in computer jobs report experiencing gender-related discrimination, compared to 16% of men (Page 12)
- 22% of working women in the U.S. say they have experienced sexual harassment at work, compared to 7% of men (Page 13)
- Women in STEM are more likely than men to regard sexual harassment as a problem in their workplace (36% vs. 28%), especially in majority-male settings (48%) and computer jobs (42%) (Page 13)
- 62% of black STEM workers report experiencing discrimination due to their race or ethnicity, compared to 42% of Hispanics and 13% of whites (Page 14)
- Black STEM workers are less likely than white workers to perceive fair treatment in hiring (43% vs. 78%) and promotions (37% vs. 75%) (Page 15)
- Employment in STEM occupations grew 79% since 1990, from 9.7 million to 17.3 million, with computer occupations seeing the largest growth at 338% (Page 16)
- Women account for a majority of healthcare practitioners and technicians (75%) but are underrepresented in computer (25%) and engineering (14%) positions (Page 16)
- Women make up 41% of STEM workers with professional or doctoral degrees (Page 17)
- Blacks make up 9% of STEM workers (vs. 11% of the U.S. workforce), Hispanics 7% (vs. 16%), while Asians are overrepresented at 17% of college-educated STEM workers (vs. 10% of all college-educated workers) (Page 17)
- About 69% of women who majored in health professions work in health-related occupations, compared to 61% of men; women are less likely than men to work in computer (38% vs. 53%) or engineering (24% vs. 30%) jobs (Page 18)
- 71% of U.S. adults see STEM jobs as offering better compensation, and 58% consider them to attract more qualified young people (Page 19)
- Women in STEM are more likely than men to prioritize jobs focused on helping others (59% vs. 31%), while men value higher pay and promotion opportunities more (Page 20)
- 39% of Americans consider lack of encouragement a major reason for fewer women in STEM, while 41% cite this for blacks and Hispanics; 42% believe limited access to quality education is a major factor for underrepresentation of blacks and Hispanics (Page 21)
- 72% of Black STEM workers believe racial/ethnic discrimination is a major reason for underrepresentation, compared to 27% of whites and 28% of Asians; 48% of women in STEM cite gender discrimination as a major factor (Page 22)
- 25% of Americans rate K-12 STEM education as above average, while 43% rate it as average and 30% as below average (Page 23)
- STEM employment grew 79% since 1990, with computer jobs increasing by 338%; women make up 50% of all STEM workers overall, but are underrepresented in computer (25%) and engineering (14%) jobs (Page 24)
- The gender wage gap is wider in STEM occupations than in non-STEM jobs (Page 24)

This page from a Pew Research Center report discusses the demographic composition of the STEM workforce, focusing on gender and racial/ethnic representation. It highlights that women are underrepresented in STEM despite gains among those with advanced degrees, making up 41% of STEM workers with professional or doctoral degrees. Black and Hispanic workers are significantly underrepresented relative to their share of the overall U.S. workforce (9% and 7% of STEM workers vs. 11% and 16% overall), while Asians are overrepresented, particularly among college-educated workers (17% of college-educated STEM workers vs. 10% of all college-educated workers). The page also defines the broad-based STEM job classification used in the analysis, which includes health-related occupations but excludes educators due to data limitations. A key finding is that STEM jobs generally require higher educational attainment, with only 33% of college-educated workers having majored in a STEM field.

**Text Evidence:**
- Women are roughly four-in-ten (41%) of all STEM workers with a professional or doctoral degree.
- Blacks make up 11% of the U.S. workforce but represent 9% of STEM workers.
- Hispanics comprise 16% of the U.S. workforce but only 7% of all STEM workers.
- Asians are overrepresented: 17% of college-educated STEM workers are Asian, compared to 10% of all college-educated workers.
- The definition of a STEM job includes life sciences, physical and Earth sciences, engineering and architecture, computer and math occupations, and health-related occupations.
- Educators specializing in STEM subjects were not identified in the American Community Survey analysis.
- Among college-educated workers, one-in-three (33%) majored in a STEM field.

The reasons why half of college-educated workers with STEM-related training turn to jobs elsewhere are likely complicated. Among college-educated workers, those who majored in a health professions field are more likely than those who majored in other STEM fields to be working in a job directly related to their degree. Diversity in the STEM workforce varies widely across jobs As the U.S. has transformed rapidly to an information-based economy, employment in science, technology, engineering and math occupations has grown – outpacing overall job growth. Since 1990, STEM employment has grown  $79\%$  (9.7 million to 17.3 million) and computer jobs have seen a whopping  $338\%$  increase over the same period. Using a broad definition of the STEM workforce, women make up half (50%) of all U.S. workers in STEM occupations, though their presence varies widely across occupational clusters and educational levels. Women account for the majority of healthcare practitioners and technicians but are underrepresented in several other STEM occupational clusters, particularly in computer jobs and engineering. While there has been significant progress for women in the life and physical sciences since 1990, the share of women has been roughly stable in other STEM occupational clusters and has actually gone down 7 percentage points in the area with the largest job growth over this period: computer occupations, a job cluster that includes computer scientists, systems analysts, software developers, information systems managers and programmers. Gains in women's representation in STEM jobs have been concentrated among women holding advanced degrees, although women still tend to be underrepresented among such workers. Black and Hispanic workers continue to be underrepresented in the STEM workforce. Blacks make up  $11\%$  of the U.S. workforce overall but represent  $9\%$  of STEM workers, while Hispanics comprise  $16\%$  of the U.S. workforce but only  $7\%$  of all STEM workers. And among employed adults with a bachelor's degree or higher, blacks are just  $7\%$  and Hispanics are  $6\%$  of the STEM workforce. Asians are overrepresented in the STEM workforce, relative to their overall share of the workforce, especially among college-educated workers:  $17\%$  of college-educated STEM workers are Asian, compared with  $10\%$  of all workers with a college degree. The representation of women, blacks and Hispanics holds pocketbook implications for workers. This page from the Pew Research Center discusses diversity in the U.S. STEM workforce, highlighting significant disparities across gender, race, and educational levels. It reports that while women make up 50% of all STEM workers overall, their representation varies widely, with underrepresentation in computer and engineering jobs despite gains in life and physical sciences. Black and Hispanic workers are also underrepresented, making up 9% and 7% of STEM workers respectively, compared to their 11% and 16% share of the overall workforce. In contrast, Asians are overrepresented, particularly among college-educated STEM workers at 17%. The text emphasizes that these demographic imbalances have economic consequences, as STEM jobs offer higher earnings but the gender wage gap is wider in STEM than in non-STEM fields.

**Text Evidence:**
- STEM employment grew 79% (9.7 million to 17.3 million) since 1990.
- Computer jobs saw a 338% increase over the same period.
- Women make up 50% of all U.S. workers in STEM occupations.
- Women's share in computer occupations has decreased by 7 percentage points since 1990.
- Blacks represent 9% of STEM workers (vs. 11% of the overall workforce).
- Hispanics represent 7% of STEM workers (vs. 16% of the overall workforce).
- Among college-educated workers, 17% of STEM workers are Asian (vs. 10% of all college graduates).
- STEM workers earn significantly more than non-STEM workers, even after controlling for education.
- The gender wage gap is wider in STEM occupations than in non-STEM jobs.

The pattern is similar for blacks and Hispanics, who also tend to be concentrated in less lucrative STEM jobs, widening the measured earnings disparity. One potential barrier for those wishing to enter the STEM workforce is the generally higher level of educational attainment required for such positions. Among college-educated workers, one-in-three (33%) majored in a STEM field. But only about half (52%) of those with college training in a STEM field are currently employed in a STEM job. The reasons about half of college-educated workers with STEM-related training turn to jobs elsewhere are likely complicated. Some may have found their skills and training to be applicable to and rewarded in a non-STEM occupation (such as banking or finance). pages.ocr_text: Defining STEM workers with a wide-angle lens This analysis uses a broad definition of the STEM workforce and is based solely on occupation, as classified in the U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey. As defined, here, the STEM workforce includes 74 occupations including computer and mathematical occupations, engineers and architects, physical scientists, life scientists, and health-related jobs such as healthcare practitioners and technicians (but not health care support workers such as nursing aides and medical assistants). As such, it includes workers with associate degrees and other credentials as well as those with bachelor's and advanced degrees. There is no standard definition of STEM workers. Other analyses of STEM workers include somewhat different occupations (see, for example, the Economics and Statistics Administration of the U.S. Department of Commerce). The National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics focuses on those with a college degree or more education in their surveys; UNESCO studies on global diversity issues in STEM focus even more narrowly on researchers with advanced degrees working in STEM. Including healthcare practitioners and technicians as STEM occupations has broad ramifications for the key findings. There are 9.0 million health-related jobs, comprising  $52\%$  of the STEM workforce. Healthcare practitioners and technicians are largely women, thus their inclusion boosts the overall representation of women in the STEM workforce. These health-related occupations also have somewhat larger shares of black workers and smaller shares of Asian workers compared with other STEM occupations, which affects the racial and ethnic composition of the overall STEM workforce. Among college-educated workers who majored in a STEM field during their undergraduate education, those who majored in health professions are significantly more likely to work in a STEM occupation, so their inclusion increases figures on the retention of STEM-trained workers. Social scientists are not included as a STEM occupation in this study, although other studies sometimes classify social sciences as a STEM job. As a practical matter, doing so makes little difference in the overall portrait of the STEM workforce because less than  $1\%$  of the workforce (about 280,000 workers in 2016) are classified as social scientists based on the Standard Occupational Classification system. See the sidebar on page 33 for more on the characteristics of social scientists in the workforce. The Census data used do not identify the subject matter expertise for postsecondary teachers, therefore, these workers are not included in the STEM workforce. As a practical matter, this omission does not appear to change the overall portrait of STEM workers, as others estimate that only  $1\%$  of those who majored in a STEM field are in academic jobs in colleges and universities. See the Appendix for characteristics of those in postsecondary teaching occupations.

This page from the Pew Research Center discusses gender representation in STEM and social science fields, highlighting trends in women's educational attainment and occupational distribution. It notes that while women make up roughly 80% of healthcare practitioners with master's degrees or less, they comprise only 45% of health-related workers with professional or doctoral degrees. The biggest growth in women's representation has been among STEM workers with advanced degrees, particularly doctoral degrees, where the share of women increased from 27% in 1990 to 41% today. The page also details that about 5.8 million (12%) college-educated workers majored in social sciences, with psychology being the most popular major (35%). However, very few social science majors work as social scientists (3%), with most employed in social services, legal, education, management, business, finance, or STEM occupations. Social scientists are highly educated, with 97% holding at least a bachelor's degree and 82% having advanced degrees.

**Text Evidence:**
- Among healthcare practitioners and technicians with a master's degree or less, roughly eight-in-ten are women.
- Among health-related workers with a professional or doctoral degree, 45% are women.
- The share of women among doctoral or professional degree holders in the overall STEM workforce has climbed from 27% in 1990 to 41% today.
- The share of women among STEM workers with a bachelor's degree (but no advanced degree) has ticked up from 43% in 1990 to 47%.
- About 5.8 million (or 12%) of today's college-educated workers majored in the social sciences.
- Psychology majors comprise the single largest group of those who majored in a social science field (35%).
- Very few workers (3%) who majored in the social sciences are employed as social scientists.
- The majority of social science majors work in the cluster of social services, legal and education (30%) or in management, business and finance occupations (26%).
- Another 12% of social science majors are employed in a STEM occupation.
- 97% of those in social science jobs have completed at least a bachelor's degree, and 82% have finished an advanced degree.
- Of the roughly 280,000 workers employed as social scientists in 2016, 80% were white, 8% were Hispanic, 5% were black, and 5% were Asian.
- Women currently make up 63% of social scientists, up from 54% in 2000 and 50% in 1990.
- Among college-educated workers who majored in the social sciences, 54% are women.

**Visual Evidence:**

This pattern generally holds within occupational clusters as well. Among healthcare practitioners and technicians with a master's degree or less, roughly eight-in-ten are women. By contrast, among health-related workers with a professional or doctoral degree,  $45\%$  are women. See Appendix for details by occupation.

At the same time, the biggest growth in women's representation since 1990 has been among STEM workers with advanced degrees, doctoral degrees in particular; this aligns with women's broader gains in educational attainment during this period. The share of women among doctoral or professional degree holders in the overall STEM workforce has climbed from  $27\%$  in 1990 to  $41\%$  today. The share of women among STEM workers with a bachelor's degree (but no advanced degree) has ticked up from  $43\%$  in 1990 to  $47\%$ , on par with the overall share of women in the workforce  $(47\%)$ .
Social sciences are a popular college major but comprise a small occupational group

About 5.8 million (or  $12\%$ ) of today's college-educated workers majored in the social sciences. Psychology majors comprise the single largest group of those who majored in a social science field  $(35\%)$ . The next most popular social science majors are political science  $(19\%)$  and economics  $(16\%)$ .

Very few workers (3%) who majored in the social sciences are employed as social scientists (based on the Standard Occupational Classification system). The majority work in the cluster of social services, legal and education (30%) or in management, business and finance occupations (26%). Another 12% of social science majors are employed in a STEM occupation.

Those in social science occupations are far more likely to be college-educated than workers in other occupational clusters:  $97\%$  of those in social science jobs have completed at least a bachelor's degree, and  $82\%$  have finished an advanced degree (a third hold a doctoral degree). Of the roughly 280,000 workers employed as social scientists in 2016,  $80\%$  were white,  $8\%$  were Hispanic,  $5\%$  were black and  $5\%$  were Asian. Women currently make up  $63\%$  of social scientists, up from  $54\%$  in 2000 and  $50\%$  in 1990. Among college-educated workers who majored in the social sciences,  $54\%$  are women.

This page from the Pew Research Center presents data on racial and ethnic representation in STEM occupations in the U.S. It highlights that whites (69%) and Asians (13%) are overrepresented in the STEM workforce, while blacks (9%) and Hispanics (7%) are underrepresented compared to their shares in the overall workforce. The text details how diversity has increased since 1990, when 83% of STEM workers were white. A bar chart visually compares the percentage of employed individuals by race/ethnicity across various STEM job clusters, showing significant variation, particularly with higher representation of black and Hispanic workers in health-related fields like nursing and technician roles. The source is a 2014-2016 American Community Survey analysis.

**Text Evidence:**
- The majority of STEM workers in the U.S. are white (69%), followed by Asians (13%), blacks (9%), and Hispanics (7%).
- In 1990, 83% of STEM workers were white, 6% were Asian, 7% were black, and 4% were Hispanic.
- Blacks and Hispanics are underrepresented in most STEM occupations, while whites and Asians are overrepresented.
- Health technician and nursing jobs have high shares of black or Hispanic workers, such as 37% of licensed practical nurses.
- In physical sciences, blacks and Hispanics comprise 22% of chemical technicians but only 14% of chemists and materials scientists.

Among mathematical workers,  $19 \%$ of operations research analysts are black or Hispanic, compared with just  $5 \%$ of actuaries. Whites are overrepresented among STEM workers relative to their share in the total workforce. Asians (including both men and women) are also overrepresented among STEM workers compared with their share in the total workforce, particularly among STEM workers with a postgraduate degree. For details, see Appendix. Asians are overrepresented across all STEM occupational groups with higher than average shares among computer workers and life scientists, accounting for  $19\%$  of workers in both of these fields, which is much higher than their share in the workforce overall (6%). The share of Asians in STEM jobs varies substantially within occupational groups, however. For example, in engineering jobs the share of Asians ranges from  $30\%$  among computer hardware engineers to  $2\%$  among surveying and mapping technicians. Among healthcare practitioners and technicians, about one-in-five physicians and surgeons  $(21\%)$  are Asian. But Asians comprise a far smaller share of veterinarians  $(3\%)$  and emergency medical technicians and paramedics  $(2\%)$ . About one-in-five (19%) STEM workers in the U.S. are foreign born, broadly similar to the share in the overall workforce (18%). The vast majority of the Asian STEM workforce is foreign born (82%) as is the Asian workforce overall in the U.S. (81%). Black STEM workers, however, are more likely to be foreign born than black workers overall (22% vs. 14%). Hispanics working in STEM jobs are far less likely than those in the workforce overall to be foreign born (32% of Hispanic STEM workers are foreign born, compared with 54% of all employed Hispanics ages 25 and older).

This page from the Pew Research Center presents data on earnings disparities between STEM and non-STEM workers, highlighting that STEM workers earn significantly more. It features a line chart showing median annual earnings for full-time, year-round workers aged 25 and older from 1990 to 2016, demonstrating that STEM earnings have increased while non-STEM earnings have remained flat. The text provides specific figures, noting that in 2016, median STEM earnings were $71,000 compared to $43,000 for non-STEM workers, representing a two-thirds higher income. The document also breaks down earnings within the STEM field, showing that computer, mathematical, and engineering roles earn more than healthcare practitioners.

**Text Evidence:**
- The typical STEM worker earns significantly more than non-STEM workers, with the gap widening since 1990.
- In 2016, median earnings for STEM occupations were $71,000, while non-STEM workers earned $43,000.
- After adjusting for inflation, STEM earnings have increased since 1990, while non-STEM earnings have been relatively flat.
- Earnings vary among STEM workers: computer, mathematical, and engineering/architects earn between $81,100 and $83,000, while healthcare practitioners and technicians earn $61,000.

**Visual Evidence:**

This page from the Pew Research Center presents data on earnings disparities in STEM versus non-STEM occupations, focusing on differences by education level and gender. It highlights that STEM workers earn more than similarly educated non-STEM workers across all educational categories, with a significant pay gap between men and women in STEM fields. The text also notes that while women in STEM earn less than men in STEM, they still earn more than women in non-STEM jobs. A bar chart visually compares median annual earnings for full-time, year-round workers aged 25 and older across various education levels, distinguishing between STEM and non-STEM employment.

**Text Evidence:**
- STEM workers earn significantly more than non-STEM workers with similar education levels.
- Among those with some college education, STEM workers earn $54,745 compared to $40,505 for non-STEM workers, a 26% difference.
- Women in STEM earned a median of $60,828 in 2016, which is 72% of men's median earnings of $84,000 in STEM.
- The gender pay gap is larger in STEM (women earn 72% of men's earnings) than in non-STEM (women earn 79% of men's earnings).
- Women in non-STEM occupations have median earnings of $38,480.

This page from a Pew Research Center report analyzes the gender earnings gap within the STEM workforce, highlighting that the overall 72% gap is influenced by occupational and educational differences. The text explains that men are more likely to work in higher-paying computer and engineering roles, while women are overrepresented in lower-paying healthcare positions. A bar chart visually breaks down the median annual earnings of women as a percentage of men's earnings across various STEM occupations and education levels, showing significant variation. Key findings include that the gap has remained stable since 1990 and is widest for those with professional or doctoral degrees (73%) and high school or less education (66%).

**Text Evidence:**
- The overall gender earnings gap in the STEM workforce is 72%.
- The gap has not changed over the past 25 years; it was also 72% in 1990.
- Among full-time, year-round workers, the gap varies by occupation: 87% for computer workers, 83% for engineers/architects, and 74% for healthcare practitioners/technicians.
- The gender pay gap is widest for STEM workers with professional or doctoral degrees (73%) and those with high school or less education (66%).
- Women are more likely than men to be in lower-paying healthcare practitioner and technician positions.

One factor that may be attracting STEM college majors to work outside of the STEM workforce is the high earnings potential of jobs in management, business and finance occupations. Most Americans believe STEM jobs pay better, but few see them as offering more flexibility for family time Americans have mixed views of how careers in science, technology, engineering and math compare to jobs in other industries. About half or more of the general public – whether they are employed in STEM or non-STEM jobs – believe that STEM jobs pay better, attract more of the brightest young people and are more well-respected. But roughly half of Americans say these jobs are difficult to get into, while only  $18\%$  believe careers in STEM have more flexibility for balancing work and family than jobs in other industries. That flexibility is an important factor in choosing a job for both men and women in STEM, as well as those working in other areas. For the most part, men and women in STEM look for similar job qualities; one notable exception is that  $59\%$  of women tend to value jobs that help others, compared with  $31\%$  of men. Interviews with people working in STEM fields highlight the sometimes subtle ways that women feel they are treated differently at work.[33] The Pew Research Center survey finds overall, men and women in STEM see behaviors that help or hurt them to get ahead in the workplace somewhat differently. Men in STEM jobs see more advantage in working harder than others, being assertive, and being vocal about their accomplishments at work. Among women, those who work in majority-male settings are more likely than other women in STEM occupations to think these behaviors help them get ahead in their job. And, women in majority-male work settings are particularly likely to say they need to prove themselves at least some of the time at work in order to be respected by their coworkers. Majorities of Americans see jobs in STEM as better compensated or better at attracting young talent compared with other industry sectors About seven-in-ten Americans (71%) believe that jobs in STEM have higher salaries than those in other fields. More broadly, though, Americans have mixed views of how careers in STEM stand up against other sectors. Some  $58\%$  of U.S. adults say that jobs in STEM attract more of "the brightest and most qualified young people." And half of Americans (50%) say that careers in STEM "offer more opportunities for advancement," a similar share (49%) believe that STEM jobs are more difficult to get into.

Women in STEM see more gender disparities at work, especially those in computer jobs, majority-male workplaces There are wide gaps between men and women working in science, technology, engineering and math jobs when it comes to perceptions of fair treatment for women at work and experiences of workplace discrimination. Women in STEM jobs are much more likely than men in such jobs to say they have experienced discrimination at work because of their gender and to consider discrimination a major reason that more women are not working in STEM. While the majority of STEM workers say their gender has made no particular difference in their success, women in STEM jobs are more inclined than men to say their gender has made it harder for them to succeed at work. Those that feel this way raise a number of concerns including pay gaps and unequal treatment from their coworkers stemming from gender stereotypes. Experiences with workplace discrimination and concerns about gender inequities are more pronounced among women working in computer positions; among those working in workplaces where men outnumber women; and among women with advanced degrees, more of whom presumably work in higher level, professional positions compared with other women in STEM jobs. Although a higher share of women in STEM jobs say they have experienced at least one form of discrimination at work because of their gender, similar shares of women in STEM jobs and non-STEM jobs say they have personally experienced sexual harassment. Women in STEM jobs also tend to share similar perspectives with working women in non-STEM jobs when it comes to the value of gender diversity and the amount of attention paid to gender diversity at work.

Women in STEM see more gender disparities at work, especially those in computer jobs, majority-male workplaces There are wide gaps between men and women working in science, technology, engineering and math jobs when it comes to perceptions of fair treatment for women at work and experiences of workplace discrimination. Women in STEM jobs are much more likely than men in such jobs to say they have experienced discrimination at work because of their gender and to consider discrimination a major reason that more women are not working in STEM. While the majority of STEM workers say their gender has made no particular difference in their success, women in STEM jobs are more inclined than men to say their gender has made it harder for them to succeed at work. Those that feel this way raise a number of concerns including pay gaps and unequal treatment from their coworkers stemming from gender stereotypes. Experiences with workplace discrimination and concerns about gender inequities are more pronounced among women working in computer positions; among those working in workplaces where men outnumber women; and among women with advanced degrees, more of whom presumably work in higher level, professional positions compared with other women in STEM jobs. Although a higher share of women in STEM jobs say they have experienced at least one form of discrimination at work because of their gender, similar shares of women in STEM jobs and non-STEM jobs say they have personally experienced sexual harassment. Women in STEM jobs also tend to share similar perspectives with working women in non-STEM jobs when it comes to the value of gender diversity and the amount of attention paid to gender diversity at work.

This page from the Pew Research Center presents findings from a 2017 survey on American attitudes toward gender diversity in the workplace. The main text and two charts show that a majority of U.S. adults (78% combined) consider gender diversity important, with 52% viewing it as "extremely" or "very" important. The primary reasons cited for its importance are providing other perspectives (46%), giving people an equal opportunity to succeed (43%), and making good business sense by increasing the supply of potential workers (33%). Americans' level of support for gender diversity depends, in part, on their own gender. Whereas more than half of women in STEM jobs and non-STEM jobs alike believe that such diversity is highly important (61% and 56%, respectively), fewer men in STEM and non-STEM jobs say the same (49% and 43%, respectively). Those who hold advanced degrees, whether they work in STEM or non-STEM jobs, express more support for the importance of gender diversity, on average. Similar shares of women and men, in both STEM and non-STEM jobs, share that assessment. Men in STEM jobs are about twice as likely to think there is too much attention given to gender diversity (13% vs. 5% of women in STEM jobs) in their workplace. <section_card>
SECTION: 4. Blacks in STEM jobs are especially concerned about diversity and discrimination in the workplace (Pages 71-85)

TOPICS: racial and ethnic diversity in STEM, workplace discrimination, underrepresentation of minorities, perceptions of fairness in hiring and promotion, early education access, role models, public opinion on STEM education

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- Blacks and Hispanics are underrepresented in STEM jobs relative to their presence in the overall U.S. workforce, especially among those with a bachelor's degree or higher (Page 71)
- Black STEM workers are particularly concerned about insufficient attention to diversity, experience high rates of discrimination, and believe they are not treated fairly in hiring and promotion (Page 71)
- Among STEM workers, blacks stand out for their concerns about too little attention to increasing diversity, high rates of workplace discrimination, and beliefs that blacks are not usually met with fair treatment in hiring and promotion (Page 71)
- Blacks in STEM share common ground with Asians and, to a lesser extent, Hispanics, who are all much less likely than whites to believe members of their own group are usually treated fairly, particularly regarding promotion and advancement (Page 71)
- Most blacks in STEM positions consider major underlying reasons for underrepresentation to be limited access to quality education, discrimination in recruitment and promotions, and a lack of encouragement to pursue these jobs from an early age (Page 71)
- 80% of U.S. adults say it is at least somewhat important to have racial and ethnic diversity in workplaces today; 53% categorize this as "extremely" (26%) or "very" important (27%) (Page 72)
- 9% each view it as "not too" or "not at all" important (Page 72)
- 45% of U.S. adults say providing other perspectives contributes to organizational success (Page 72)
- 45% say it gives people an equal opportunity to succeed (Page 72)
- 34% say it makes good business sense by increasing the supply of potential workers (Page 72)
- The survey was conducted from July 11-Aug. 10, 2017 (Page 72)
- Blacks employed in STEM are far more likely than whites to say diversity is extremely or very important (84% vs. 49%, a difference of 35 percentage points) (Page 73)
- Among all U.S. adults, 53% say it is extremely/very important to have racial and ethnic diversity in workplaces (Page 73)
- There were not enough Asian respondents in non-STEM jobs to be analyzed separately (Page 73)
- 65% of employed adults say their workplace pays the right amount of attention to increasing racial and ethnic diversity (Page 74)
- 22% believe there is too little focus, and 11% say too much attention is given (Page 74)
- 57% of Black STEM employees say their workplace pays too little attention to diversity (Page 74)
- 15% of White STEM employees say the same (Page 74)
- 57% of Black STEM employees feel there is too little attention, compared to 43% of Black non-STEM employees (Page 74)
- 23% of Hispanic STEM employees feel there is too little attention, compared to 37% of Hispanic non-STEM employees (Page 74)
- Blacks and Hispanics made up 27% of the overall U.S. workforce in 2016 but only 16% of STEM workers (Page 75)
- 52% of STEM workers believe limited access to quality education is a major reason for underrepresentation (Page 75)
- 45% attribute the disparities to a lack of encouragement at an early age (Page 75)
- 34% of STEM workers attribute underrepresentation to blacks and Hispanics not believing in their ability to succeed (Page 76)
- 32% cite lack of role models and racial/ethnic discrimination as major reasons (Page 76)
- 54% of STEM employees say blacks and Hispanics being less interested is not at all a reason for employment gaps (Page 76)
- 72% of black STEM employees say discrimination is a major reason, compared to 27% of white employees and 28% of Asians (Page 76)
- 43% of Hispanic STEM employees cite discrimination as a major reason (Page 76)
- Blacks in STEM are far more likely than other groups to attribute underrepresentation to lack of access to quality education or early encouragement (Page 76)
- People in STEM jobs are more likely to cite lack of access to quality education (52% vs. 42%), lack of encouragement (45% vs. 40%), and lack of black and Hispanic role models (32% vs. 27%) as major reasons for underrepresentation (Page 77)
- Blacks in STEM jobs are about 20 percentage points more likely than blacks in non-STEM jobs to think lack of quality schooling and lack of encouragement are major reasons (Page 77)
- Blacks in STEM jobs are more likely than those in non-STEM occupations to think discrimination is a major reason (72% vs. 58%) (Page 77)
- Overall, one-quarter of workers say they have experienced any of eight forms of discrimination in the workplace due to their race or ethnicity (Page 77)
- 62% of Black STEM employees say they have experienced discrimination at work, compared to 44% of Asians and 42% of Hispanics in STEM jobs (Page 77)
- 62% of black STEM workers have experienced any type of racial/ethnic discrimination at work (Page 78)
- 45% of black STEM workers say they have been treated as not competent because of their race (Page 78)
- 29% of black STEM workers have felt isolated in their workplace because of their race (Page 78)
- Hispanics in STEM and non-STEM jobs are equally likely to report experiencing workplace discrimination (42% each) (Page 78)
- One-in-five STEM workers who say their race has hampered their success point to treatment from coworkers as the reason (Page 79)
- 71% of white STEM workers say their race or ethnicity has made no difference to success; 22% say it has made it easier; 5% say it has made it harder (Page 79)
- Blacks and Asians in STEM jobs, followed by Hispanics, are more likely than white STEM workers to say their race or ethnicity has made it harder to find success (Page 79)
- 1-in-8 Americans (13%) say their race or ethnicity has made job success harder (Page 79)
- Among STEM workers who say their race or ethnicity has made it harder to succeed, 19% cite treatment from coworkers (Page 80)
- 19% say they are affected by reverse discrimination (Page 80)
- 14% cite general bias against racial and ethnic minorities (Page 80)
- 12% report hiring, promotion, and salary barriers (Page 80)
- 9% of the group describe feeling unwelcome in their workplace (Page 81)
- A similar share (9%) say they are held to different standards than coworkers (Page 81)
- About two-in-ten STEM workers (19%) said their race has made success harder due to reverse discrimination (Page 81)
- Two quotes from white male STEM professionals express feelings of being passed over for minorities (Page 82)
- 86% of STEM workers believe Whites are 'Usually treated fairly' in recruitment/hiring; 83% believe this about promotion/advancement (Page 82)
- 78% of STEM workers believe Asian Americans are 'Usually treated fairly' in recruitment/hiring; 73% believe this about promotion/advancement (Page 82)
- 72% of STEM workers believe Hispanics are 'Usually treated fairly' in recruitment/hiring; 67% believe this about promotion/advancement (Page 82)
- 71% of STEM workers believe Blacks are 'Usually treated fairly' in recruitment/hiring; 67% believe this about promotion/advancement (Page 82)
- 43% of Black STEM workers believe Blacks are generally treated fairly in recruitment; 37% believe this about advancement (Page 83)
- 78% of white STEM workers believe Blacks are usually treated fairly in hiring; 75% believe this about advancement (Page 83)
- 53% of Asian STEM workers believe Asian Americans are usually treated fairly in promotion and advancement; 79% of white STEM workers hold this view (Page 83)
- 59% of Hispanic STEM workers believe Hispanics are usually treated fairly in promotion and advancement; 74% of white STEM workers agree (Page 83)
- 72% of Hispanic STEM workers and 78% of white STEM workers believe Hispanics are usually treated fairly in hiring processes (Page 83)
- A Black woman engineer, 57, states that STEM needs to be emphasized as early as elementary school (Page 84)
- A Black woman nurse, 49, advises introducing STEM early and providing rigorous college preparation (Page 84)
- A Black man systems engineer, 30, suggests making Black men in STEM visible to younger generations (Page 84)
- A Hispanic woman nurse, 68, highlights the need for government support and belief in science and technology (Page 84)
- An Asian woman biological researcher, 24, recommends highlighting successful examples from the same ethnicity (Page 84)
- An Asian woman physical scientist, 26, calls for better promotion of jobs with higher pay and flexible work-life balance (Page 84)
- A Hispanic man respiratory therapist, 58, advocates for hands-on learning where students can see an end result (Page 84)
- A White woman K-12 math teacher, 42, stresses the need to make STEM subjects more accessible to girls (Page 84)
- A White woman software testing consultant, 55, recommends teaching about diverse female role models like Grace Hopper and Marie Pasteur (Page 84)
- Most Americans give positive ratings for how well K-12 public schools teach reading, writing, and mathematics (Page 85)
- A large majority of Americans say K-12 STEM education is no better than average compared with other developed nations (Page 85)
- Only a minority of the public considers U.S. higher education in STEM to be at least above average compared with other industrialized nations (Page 85)
- A majority of Americans attribute problems in K-12 STEM education to limited parental involvement, student work ethic, and diminished interest in learning (Page 85)
- Many adults also believe such problems are due to teaching methods and curriculum emphasis on meeting state standards (Page 85)
- Parents of students in public schools generally see local schools in a positive light (Page 85)
- Some seven-in-ten parents say local K-12 public schools do an excellent or good job (Page 85)

pages.summary:
This page from a Pew Research Center report examines public perceptions of K-12 STEM education in the United States. It presents data showing that while most Americans rate their local schools positively for teaching basic skills like reading, writing, and math, opinions on STEM education are more mixed. A large majority of U.S. adults believe K-12 STEM education is no better than average compared to other developed nations. The page includes four bar charts comparing the ratings of U.S. adults and parents of public school students on various educational outcomes, including teaching basics, college preparation, vocational skills, and critical thinking. The survey was conducted from July 11 to August 10, 2017.

**Text Evidence:**
- Most Americans give positive ratings for how well K-12 public schools teach reading, writing, and mathematics.
- A large majority of Americans say K-12 STEM education is no better than average compared with other developed nations.
- Only a minority of the public considers U.S. higher education in STEM to be at least above average compared with other industrialized nations.
- A majority of Americans attribute problems in K-12 STEM education to limited parental involvement, student work ethic, and diminished interest in learning.
- Many adults also believe such problems are due to teaching methods and curriculum emphasis on meeting state standards.
- Parents of students in public schools generally see local schools in a positive light.
- Some seven-in-ten parents say local K-12 public schools do an excellent or good job.

**Visual Evidence:**
<table_summary>Table: Most Americans say K-12 public schools do a good job teaching basics, preparing students for college - This table shows the percentage of U.S. adults and public school parents who rate their local K-12 public schools as excellent or good versus only fair or poor across four categories: Teaching reading, writing and mathematics (61% vs 36%), Providing the knowledge and skills needed for a four-year college degree (59% vs 39%), Providing the knowledge and skills needed to pursue a vocational or technical career (52% vs 45%), and Teaching critical-thinking and problem-solving skills (49% vs 49%).</table_summary>

Many Americans say they liked math and science in school, thought about a STEM career One of the first ways Americans encounter science, technology, engineering and math is through their early education. And many look back fondly at their science and math classes during this time in their lives. Three-quarters of Americans say they liked science classes in grades K-12, citing labs and activities as a key reason why. And, a smaller majority recalls liking math classes in grades K-12. STEM workers are more likely than those working in other fields to say they liked science or math classes in school, but still more than four-in-ten non-STEM workers say they liked both subjects in grades K-12. Many of those who work in occupations outside of STEM also say they were once interested in pursuing a job or career in STEM. pages.ocr_text: "Middle-skills" STEM workers are particularly likely to have had additional training "Middle-skills" jobs, which require additional training beyond a high school education but not a four-year college degree, make-up an important part of the STEM workforce. Middle-skills jobs are particularly common in computer technology and health care. About three-in-ten STEM workers (28%) have some college experience (including an associate degree) but no bachelor's degree. This is a similar share to those employed in non-STEM occupations (31%). Among those with some college experience, STEM workers earn 35% more than their non-STEM counterparts ($54,745 vs. $40,505). See Chapter 1. STEM middle-skills workers are distinct from middle-skills workers in other occupations because they are more likely to have additional educational training that is directly related to their job. STEM workers are more likely than non-STEM workers to have completed any vocational or technical training, a certificate, or apprenticeship. Among those with some college experience or an associate degree, about seven-in-ten STEM workers (69%) say they have completed this kind of training, compared with about half of non-STEM workers (49%). In addition, among workers with an associate degree, STEM workers are more likely than workers in other occupations to say their job is closely related to their education. Some  $77\%$  of STEM workers with an associate degree say their job is very closely related to their degree. In contrast, about three-in-ten  $(28\%)$  of those working in other occupations say their associate degree is closely related to their current job, while a larger share  $(42\%)$  say their degree is not related or not very closely related to their job. Similarly, STEM workers with an associate degree are about three times more likely than their non-STEM counterparts to say they use the skills and knowledge from their degree in their current job all the time (73% vs 24%).

Methodology The analysis in this report comes from two sources: 1) Pew Research Center analysis of the Census Bureau's American Community Survey (IPUMS) and the 1990 and 2000 decennial censuses and 2) a nationally representative survey conducted from July 11 to Aug. 10, 2017, among a sample of 4,914 adults 18 years of age or older. The margin of error for the full sample is plus or minus 2.7 percentage points. The survey was conducted by the GfK Group in English and Spanish using KnowledgePanel, its nationally representative online research panel. KnowledgePanel members are recruited through probability sampling methods and include those with internet access and those who did not have internet access at the time of their recruitment (KnowledgePanel provides internet access for those who do not have it and a device to access the internet when they join the panel, if needed). A combination of random-digit dialing (RDD) and address-based sampling (ABS) methodologies have been used to recruit panel members (in 2009 KnowledgePanel switched its sampling methodology for recruiting members from RDD to ABS). KnowledgePanel continually recruits new panel members throughout the year to offset panel attrition as people leave the panel. All active members of the GfK panel were eligible for inclusion in this study. PEW RESEARCH CENTER
